previous_paragraph:
The paper is structured to sequentially develop and demonstrate the proposed framework. Section 2 establishes the RTHS problem formulation and the high-fidelity transfer-system model used throughout the study. Section 3 investigates the effect of physical-substructure degradation on outer-loop stability and derives the corresponding degradation-dependent stability boundary. Section 4 provides the technical background on classical and modern robustness measures and uses this progression to introduce and formulate the NCF-based online stability indicator. Section 5 develops the controller-switching framework and examines the stability of the transition using Lyapunov criteria. Section 6 demonstrates the complete framework through an illustrative vRTHS example involving nonlinear specimen degradation and controller switching. Finally, Section 7 summarizes the main findings and conclusions.
The missing paragraph opens Section 2: Problem Formulation. Figure 1 and Figure 2 and their captions appear after it and before the next prose paragraph.
actual_paragraph: The fundamental concept of RTHS is to partition a reference structural model into two substructures. Therefore, an RTHS consists of several major components, including: (i) a numerical substructure that can be evaluated in real-time on a computer; (ii) a physical substructure excited by actuators and instrumented with sensors; and, (iii) a transfer system, comprising the controller, servo-valve and actuator hydraulics, that enforces compatibility and equilibrium interface by synchronizing the physical substructure's response with the numerical evaluated response. Figure 1 illustrates a typical RTHS scheme where the numerical substructure is subjected to a ground acceleration, agt, where dd is the calculated desired displacement from the numerical model, and fe is the measured force from the physical substructure, while Figure 2 provides a closer look inside the transfer system block. Although seismic excitation is used for illustration in this study, the proposed framework is not restricted to earthquake loading and can be applied to other external excitations, such as wind loading, by modifying the corresponding input to the numerical substructure.
